articles.title: Questions you answer with yes or no

article_json.also_called: Yes/no questions, and the helping-verb swap
article_json.one_line: This lets you turn a statement into a question that the other person can answer with *yes* or with *no*.
article_json.short_answer: Put the helping verb in front of the subject. With no helping verb, start with *do*, *does* or *did*: *Does the bus stop here?*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I turn a statement into a question?

body.text: What this kind of question asks the other person
A yes/no question hands the other person two answers to choose from. They say yes, or they say no, and either one finishes the job.
So this question needs no question word at the front. What it needs is a change of order, and English makes that change the same way every time.
Move the helping verb in front of the subject

body.caption: The helping verb jumps in front of the subject. Nothing else moves.
rows: The results will come out today.
Will the results come out today?
The bus stops at the clinic.
Does the bus stop at the clinic?
The bus stopped at the clinic.
Did the bus stop at the clinic?
footnotes: The last two rows had no helping verb, so English put one in and the main verb went back to its plain form.

body.text: In the first four rows one word moved and everything else stayed put. In the last two there was no word to move, so *does* and *did* took the time and the person, and *stops* became *stop*.

body.caption: Three boxes. The first one is the word you moved.

body.lead_in: The statement already had a helping verb in each of these. Watch which word moved to the front.

items.text: Is the ferry running today?
items.gloss: You want to know whether it is running. Yes or no settles it.

items.text: Have the results been published?
items.gloss: You want to know whether they are out yet.

items.text: Can the council refuse the application?
items.gloss: You want to know whether refusing it is allowed.

items.text: Should we book the room in advance?
items.gloss: You want advice about booking early.

items.text: Was the site closed all week?
items.gloss: You want to know whether anybody could get on to it.

body.so_what: Every one of them starts with a word taken out of the middle of a statement.

body.lead_in: None of these statements had a helping verb, so *do*, *does* or *did* went in at the front.

items.text: Does the clinic open on Saturdays?
items.gloss: You want to know whether you can go at the weekend.

items.text: Did the survey close in March?
items.gloss: You want to know whether it is too late to take part.

items.text: Do the buses run after nine?
items.gloss: You want to know whether you can get home late.

items.text: Did the panel reach a decision?
items.gloss: You want to know whether the matter is settled.

body.so_what: *Do*, *does* and *did* carry the time and the person, so the verb behind them is the plain form.

body.text: Put the helping verb in front of the subject. If the statement has no helping verb, put *do*, *does* or *did* in front and use the plain verb.

body.lead_in: One statement, four times. Only the time changes, and only the first word shows it.

items.text: Is the depot open at weekends?
items.gloss: You are asking about how things stand now.

items.text: Was the depot open last weekend?
items.gloss: You are asking about one weekend that is over.

items.gloss: You are asking about the stretch running up to today.

items.text: Will the depot be open in August?
items.gloss: You are asking about a month that has not come yet.

body.so_what: Only the first word changed. Everything behind it stayed where it was.

body.text: The verb *be* moves on its own
*Is*, *are*, *was* and *were* need no help. When one of them is the only verb in the sentence, it moves to the front by itself, and *do* never appears.

body.lead_in: There is no other verb in any of these, so *be* does the moving.

items.text: Are the seats free at the back?
items.gloss: You want to know whether you can sit there.

items.text: Was the second route cheaper?
items.gloss: You want to know which one cost less.

items.text: Is the training free for staff?
items.gloss: You want to know whether staff have to pay.

body.so_what: None of them has *do* in it, because there was already a word that could move.

body.text: Which word starts the question?

body.intro: Three questions, in this order. Stop at the first one that answers.

verdict.use: that word, moved to the front
verdict.why: *Be* is its own helping verb, so nothing needs to be put in.

steps.ask: Does it contain *have*, *will*, *can*, *must* or another helper?

verdict.use: that word, moved to the front
verdict.why: The first helper is the one that moves. Later ones stay where they are.

steps.ask: Is the statement about the past?

verdict.why: *Did* takes the past, so the verb behind it loses its past shape.

verdict.example: Does the office close at four?
verdict.why: Use *does* for *he*, *she*, *it* or one thing, and *do* for the rest.

body.text: Most sentences stop at the first two questions. The third one only comes up when the statement has no helping verb anywhere in it.
What goes wrong

body.wrong: Did the survey closed in March?
body.right: Did the survey close in March?
body.why_it_happens: The statement was *the survey closed*, and that past shape feels like part of the word. *Did* has already taken the past, so the verb behind it goes back to its plain form.
body.smallest_fix: Take the *-ed* off the main verb. Only one word in the question carries the time.

body.wrong: Does the clinic opens on Saturdays?
body.right: Does the clinic open on Saturdays?
body.why_it_happens: The statement was *the clinic opens*, and the *-s* looks like it belongs to the verb. The *-s* has moved onto *does*, and it cannot sit in two places at once.
body.smallest_fix: Take the *-s* off the main verb. *Does* is already carrying it.

body.wrong: You have sent the application form?
body.right: Have you sent the application form?
body.why_it_happens: In speech you can leave the words in statement order and raise your voice at the end, and it works. On the page there is no voice, so the order has to do the work.
body.smallest_fix: Move the helping verb to the front whenever you are writing.

body.label: One older shape you will meet in reading and should not copy

items.text: When *have* means *own*, modern English uses *do*: *Does she have a permit?*
items.example: Does the flat have a second exit?

items.text: The older British shape moves *have* itself. It sounds dated and formal.

body.heard: To make a question, put a question mark at the end and raise your voice.
also_known_as: a question mark is what makes it a question
body.truth: That works in speech and it does not work on the page. *You have sent the form?* has a question mark and is still written as a statement. What makes it a question in English is the order: the helping verb sits in front of the subject.
body.what_to_do: Move the helping verb to the front, then add the question mark. Keep the statement-with-a-question-mark shape for speech, where the rise in your voice does the same job.

body.mechanism: Chinese turns a statement into a yes/no question by adding a small word at the end, and nothing in the sentence moves.
body.wrong: The ferry is running today?
body.right: Is the ferry running today?
body.fix: Move the helping verb to the front. English has no word you can add at the end instead.

body.mechanism: Tamil marks a yes/no question with an ending added to a word, and the word order stays as it is.
body.wrong: The clinic opens on Saturdays?
body.right: Does the clinic open on Saturdays?
body.fix: Start the question with *do*, *does* or *did* when there is no other helping verb.

article_json.also_called: *Wh*-questions: the question words, and object questions
article_json.one_line: This lets you ask for one piece of information — a time, a place, a reason, a person or an amount.
article_json.short_answer: Put the question word first, then build a yes/no question behind it: *Where did the survey take place?*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I ask a question that needs a real answer, not yes or no?

body.text: What this kind of question asks for
A yes/no question offers two answers. This one leaves a hole in the sentence and asks the other person to fill it, so the answer can be anything.
The hole is marked by one word at the front, and that word says what kind of thing is missing: a time, a place, a person, a reason.

show_first.text: Why did the line close early?
How many people applied this year?

body.name_line: The word at the front is called the **question word**.
body.anchor_line: Each one names the shape of the missing piece. Answer with the wrong shape and the other person will ask again.

body.text: What each question word asks for

body.caption: Pick the word by the shape of the answer you want back.
rows: a person, in a formal letter
To whom should the form be sent?
Whose signature is on the last page?
a thing, from an open set
Which of the two routes is shorter?
How did they measure the drift?
How long has the ferry been running?
How often is the bridge inspected?
How far is the depot from the port?
What is the coast road like in winter?
What kind of survey was it?
What is the second valve for?
footnotes: *Whom* is the formal form and it belongs after a small placing word such as *to* or *for*. Everyday English uses *who*.

body.lead_in: One sentence, six holes. Only the missing piece changes.

items.text: Who approved the new timetable?
items.gloss: You want a name.

items.text: When did the council approve the new timetable?
items.gloss: You want a date.

items.text: Why did the council approve the new timetable?
items.gloss: You want the reason behind it.

items.text: How did the council approve it so quickly?
items.gloss: You want to know what made the speed possible.

body.so_what: The rest of the question stayed the same. Only the word at the front decided what came back.

body.text: Build a yes/no question, then put the word in front
There is nothing new to learn about the order. Make the yes/no question first, then set the question word in front of it and take out the piece you are asking about.

body.caption: The middle column is the whole of the work. The last move is one word.
rows: The archive is in the annexe.
The panel will meet six people.
How many people will the panel meet?

body.text: Put the question word first, then the helping verb, then the subject. If there is no helping verb, use *do*, *does* or *did*.

body.lead_in: Four questions, four helping verbs. The question word is in front of every one of them.

items.text: Where are the spare keys kept?
items.gloss: You want to know where to look for them.

items.text: Why has the second gate been locked?
items.gloss: You want the reason it is shut.

items.text: How long will the roadworks last?
items.gloss: You want to know when the road will be clear.

items.text: What did the inspectors recommend?
items.gloss: You want to know what they said should happen.

body.so_what: In every one, the word after the question word is a helping verb, and the subject comes after that.

body.text: *What* or *which*?

body.question: Do we both already know the list I am choosing from?

options.label: *what*
options.use_it_when: The set is open. You have not named the possible answers and the other person could say anything.
options.example: What caused the flooding on the coast road?

options.label: *which*
options.use_it_when: The set is known to both of you — it is in front of you, or you named it a moment ago.
options.example: Which of the two routes did they close?

a.text: What did the council fund this year?
a.means: The other person can name anything the council paid for.

b.text: Which did the council fund this year?
b.means: You both already have a short list, and you want one item off it.

a.means: Any time at all. Name one.

b.text: Which time works for you?
b.means: Two or three times have already been offered. Pick one of them.

a.text: What did you study at university?
a.means: You are asking about any subject in the world.

b.text: Which did you study, engineering or architecture?
b.means: You have named two subjects and you want one of them.

minimal_pairs.only_difference: *What* / *Which*, and the named pair that follows

a.text: What is the fastest way into town?
a.means: Any route counts, including one you have never heard of.

b.text: Which is the fastest way into town?
b.means: The routes are on a map in front of you both.

body.deciding_factor: Ask whether you could point at the answers. If you could, use *which*. If the other person could say anything, use *what*.
body.trap: You were taught that *which* is for things and *who* is for people, so you avoid *which* about people. *Which of the two candidates withdrew?* is normal English.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. The choice pays most in Speaking Part 3, where *which of these* narrows a wide question down to something you can answer.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: What means this word?
body.right: What does this word mean?
body.why_it_happens: Many languages put the question word in front and leave the rest of the sentence alone. English still needs a helping verb after the question word, and here it has to be put in.
body.smallest_fix: Add *does* after the question word and take the *-s* off the main verb.

body.wrong: Where the survey did take place?
body.right: Where did the survey take place?
body.why_it_happens: The question word went to the front, and then the rest of the sentence was left in statement order. The helping verb has to come before the subject as well.
body.smallest_fix: Swap the helping verb and the subject: *did the survey*, not *the survey did*.

body.wrong: Why did the line closed so early?
body.right: Why did the line close so early?
body.why_it_happens: The statement was *the line closed*, and the past shape feels welded to the verb. *Did* is already carrying the past, so the verb behind it goes back to its plain form.
body.smallest_fix: Take the *-ed* off the main verb.

body.heard: *Which* is for things and *who* is for people, so you cannot use *which* about people.
body.truth: *Which* is not about people or things at all. It is about whether the list is already known. *Which of the two surveyors signed it?* is normal English, because the two surveyors have already been named.
body.what_to_do: Choose *which* when you could point at the possible answers, whatever they are. Choose *what* when the other person could say anything.

body.mechanism: Spanish can leave the subject after the verb in a question, so the English order sounds like an extra step that is not needed.
body.wrong: Where lives your brother now?
body.right: Where does your brother live now?
body.fix: Put a helping verb straight after the question word, then the subject.

body.headline: Question word, helping verb, subject. In that order, every time.

articles.title: Questions where you do not use *do*

article_json.one_line: This lets you ask who or what did something, without adding a helping verb that does not belong in the sentence.
article_json.short_answer: If the question word is the doer, use no *do* and keep statement order: *Who signed the form?*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: When do I leave *do*, *does* and *did* out of a *wh*-question?

body.text: Two questions that look the same and are not
*Who called the office?* and *Who did the office call?* both start with *who* and both ask about a person. One asks for the caller. The other asks for the person on the other end.
The difference is which slot the question word is standing in. If it is standing where the doer would stand, English adds nothing at all.
When the question word is the doer, nothing moves

body.caption: The doer version has no helping verb in it, and needs none.
rows: the one it was done to
the one it was done to, in the past
footnotes: The doer rows keep the order of an ordinary statement. Only the first word tells you it is a question.

body.text: So the doer version is shorter, and it is short because nothing was taken out of the middle. The question word is sitting in the doer's own place.

body.caption: The question word fills a different slot in each one.

body.lead_in: In each of these the question word is the doer, so there is no helping verb anywhere.

body.text: When the question word is the doer, keep statement order and add no helping verb. Everything else takes a helping verb.

body.deciding_factor: Answer your own question in a full sentence. If the answer lands in front of the verb, drop the *do*.
body.trap: You have been drilled on *do*, *does* and *did* until they feel obligatory, so you put one in every question, and *Who did write it?* comes out.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. The doer version is common in Speaking Part 1 and in reading, and getting it wrong is heard at once by a listener.

body.intro: Two questions, and the first one settles most sentences.

steps.ask: Answer your own question in a full sentence. Where does the answer sit?

branches.answer: In front of the verb — *The warden locked it.*

verdict.why: The question word is standing in the doer's place, so nothing was taken out.

branches.answer: After the verb — *She locked the gate.*

steps.ask: Is there already a helping verb in the sentence?

verdict.use: that helping verb, in front of the subject
verdict.why: The helper is already there, so it moves rather than being put in.
There is nothing to move, so English puts a helper in to carry the time.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: Who did chose the site?
body.right: Who chose the site?
body.why_it_happens: Every other *wh*-question you have practised needed *did*, so it goes in by habit. Here *who* is already the doer, and nothing has been taken out for *did* to stand in for.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *did* and put the past back on the verb: *chose*.

body.wrong: Who are coming to the session tomorrow?
body.right: Who is coming to the session tomorrow?
body.why_it_happens: You expect several people, so the verb is made plural to match them. *Who* takes the singular verb whatever the answer turns out to be.
body.smallest_fix: Use *is*, *has* or *was* after *who* and *what* as the doer.

body.wrong: Who the trust appointed last year?
body.right: Who did the trust appoint last year?
body.why_it_happens: The doer version has no helping verb, so the pattern is copied across to the other one. Here *the trust* is the doer, so *who* is not, and a helper is needed.
body.smallest_fix: Put *did* after *who* and use the plain verb behind it.

body.heard: Every *wh*-question needs *do*, *does* or *did* unless there is another helping verb in it.
also_known_as: always add did to a past question
body.truth: That covers most *wh*-questions and it breaks on the commonest one of all. When the question word is the doer, there is no gap for the helper to fill, so *Who chose the site?* takes nothing.
body.what_to_do: Before you add *did*, answer your own question. If the answer goes in front of the verb, leave the helper out.

body.text: Why the question sounds unfinished without it
Many verbs carry a small placing word with them. You *wait for* a bus, *apply for* a job, *write to* somebody, *depend on* somebody. The verb is not finished without it.
When you turn one of those into a question, the small word has nowhere to go, so English leaves it standing at the end. That is not sloppy. It is the normal shape.
Leave the small word at the end

body.caption: Everyday English leaves it at the end. Moving it forward sounds formal.
rows: Which team does he report to?
To which team does he report?
For what is the grant intended?
footnotes: Both columns are correct English. The last row is stiff enough that a writer would rewrite the sentence instead.

body.text: The everyday column is what you will hear and what you should write. The formal column belongs in a letter that is already formal from the first line.

body.why_it_happens: In many languages the question word already carries the meaning that English puts in the small word, so nothing is left to say at the end. English keeps the word the verb takes, even when it lands last.

body.why_it_happens: *Whom* has been learned as the careful, correct form, so it goes in wherever a person is being asked about. *Whom* is never the doer of the verb, however formal the sentence is.

body.why_it_happens: The small word was moved to the front, which is the formal shape, and *who* stayed as it was. The two halves belong to two different registers, so the question sounds broken.

body.text: Why English does not repeat the whole sentence
Somebody asks *Have you sent the form?* Everything in that question is already shared, so repeating it back adds nothing. English keeps one word from it and leaves the rest out.
The word it keeps is the helping verb. That single word is enough to point back at the whole question, and the listener fills in the rest without noticing.

body.wrong: Have you finished the form? — Yes, I've.

body.why_it_happens: The run-together form is what you hear all day, so it comes out here as well. A short answer ends on the helping verb, and a run-together form cannot be a last word.

body.why_it_happens: Repeating the main verb feels like a fuller, more helpful answer. English brings back the helping verb instead, and the main verb is the word it leaves out.
body.smallest_fix: Use the word that started the question: *do*, *does* or *did*.

body.wrong: Have you sent the application form? — Yes, I have sent the application form.
body.right: Have you sent the application form? — Yes, I have. I sent it on Monday.
body.why_it_happens: Repeating every word looks careful and complete on paper. In speech it sounds like a translation exercise, because everything after the helping verb is already known.
body.smallest_fix: Stop after the helping verb, then add something the other person does not know yet.

body.text: Four steps, and the same four every time
A tag is a two-word question stuck on the end of a statement. It does not ask for new information. It asks the other person to come in and agree.

body.text: The tune decides what the tag means
Two speakers can say the same tag and mean opposite things. The words are identical. What separates them is whether the voice goes down at the end or up.

A plain question leaves a hole and waits. The shapes on this page do something else. They check something you already believe, or they show that you are listening, or they save words.
Five of the six belong to speech, so they are worth recognising more than producing. The first one is different, because it turns up in reading and in letters as well.

body.why_it_happens: The short shape is what you hear all day, and it feels friendly rather than lazy. On the page there is no voice and no shared context, so the missing words are missing for the reader too.

body.text: A question stops being a question when it goes inside
*Where is the archive?* is a whole question standing on its own. Put it inside *Could you tell me…* and it stops being the question. The outer sentence is the question now.
So the inside part goes back to the order a statement uses. That is the whole rule, and it is the single most persistent error in this area.

body.wrong: The study examines why did emissions rise after the ban.
body.right: The study examines why emissions rose after the ban.
body.why_it_happens: Nothing here is polite, so the rule feels as though it does not apply. It is not a politeness rule. Any question inside a sentence loses its *do*, and the time goes onto the main verb.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *did* and put the past on the main verb: *rose*.

body.wrong: I would like to know is the deposit refundable.
body.right: I would like to know whether the deposit is refundable.
body.why_it_happens: A yes/no question has no question word, so there is nothing to join it on with, and the two halves are left touching. *Whether* or *if* is the word that does the joining.
body.smallest_fix: Put *whether* in and then use statement order behind it.

body.wrong: Isn't it obvious that cities need better public transport?
body.right: Cities plainly need better public transport.
body.why_it_happens: The question sounds forceful when you read it aloud, so it feels like a strong opening. A marked essay is graded on the claim you make, and a question makes no claim.
body.smallest_fix: Turn the question into the statement it was hiding.

body.label: Three details that come up constantly, all worth learning now

items.text: The question mark follows the whole sentence, not the part inside it.
items.example: I wonder where the archive is.

items.text: *Whether* and *if* both join a yes/no question on. Before *to* and before *or not*, only *whether* works.
items.example: The panel has not decided whether to appeal.

items.text: A question word plus *to* and a verb is a short way of saying *what we should do*.
items.example: Nobody explained how to fill in the second page.

body.heard: An indirect question is a polite opening — you add *Could you tell me* and leave the rest of the question as it was.
body.truth: The opening is half of it. Behind it the words change order: the subject moves in front of the verb and *do* disappears. The same order is required in academic writing, where nothing polite is going on.
body.what_to_do: After *Could you tell me*, *Do you know*, *I wonder* or *The report examines*, write the rest as a statement. Keep the question mark only if the whole sentence is a question.

body.mechanism: Spanish keeps the verb in front of the subject inside an embedded question, so the English change of order looks like a rule with no reason behind it.
body.wrong: I do not know where is the office.
body.right: I do not know where the office is.
body.fix: Behind the wrapper, put the subject before the verb.

body.headline: Wrapper first, then a statement. No *do*, and no swapped order.

article_json.also_called: Negation with *not*, and the *do* that carries it
article_json.one_line: This lets you say that something is not the case, at any time, without moving anything else in the sentence.
article_json.short_answer: Put *not* straight after the first helping verb. If there is none, use *do not*, *does not* or *did not*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say that something did not happen?

body.text: One word, and one place for it
English says no with a single word, *not*, and that word has one address. It goes straight after the first helping verb in the sentence.
So the only real question is what to do when the sentence has no helping verb at all. English puts one in, and that is where *do*, *does* and *did* come from.
Put *not* after the first helping verb

body.text: Put *not* straight after the first helping verb. If the sentence has none, put *do*, *does* or *did* in and use the plain verb.

body.lead_in: None of these sentences had a helping verb, so one was put in to carry the *not*.

body.so_what: *Do*, *does* and *did* carry the time and the person, so the verb behind them is the plain form.

body.text: When there is no helping verb to hang *not* on

body.intro: Three questions, in this order. Stop at the first one that answers.

steps.ask: Is there already a helping verb, or *is*, *are*, *was*, *were*?

verdict.example: The office is not open on Fridays.
verdict.why: There is already a word to carry the *not*, so nothing is put in.

steps.ask: Is the sentence about the past?

verdict.example: The panel did not meet in August.
verdict.why: *Did* takes the past, so the verb behind it loses its past shape.

steps.ask: Is the subject *he*, *she*, *it*, or one thing?

verdict.example: The ferry does not run in January.
verdict.why: *Does* takes the *-s*, so the verb behind it drops it.

verdict.example: The gates do not open before eight.
verdict.why: *Do* carries the sentence and the verb stays in its plain form.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The council didn't approved the plan.
body.right: The council didn't approve the plan.
body.why_it_happens: The positive sentence was *the council approved*, and that past shape feels welded to the verb. *Did* has taken the past, and one sentence cannot carry it twice.
body.smallest_fix: Take the *-ed* off the main verb.

body.wrong: She don't work at the clinic any more.
body.right: She doesn't work at the clinic any more.
body.why_it_happens: *Don't* is the form you hear most, so it becomes the default. *Do* still has to match the subject, and with *he*, *she* or *it* the form is *does*.
body.smallest_fix: Use *doesn't* with *he*, *she*, *it* or one thing.

body.wrong: The report not includes the second site.
body.right: The report does not include the second site.
body.why_it_happens: Many languages put their negative word straight in front of the verb and need nothing else. English needs a helping verb to carry *not*, so when there is none it puts one in.
body.smallest_fix: Add *does not* and put the verb back into its plain form.

body.label: Two places where *not* sits somewhere else, both common

items.text: In an instruction, *do* appears even with *be*: *Don't be late.*
items.example: Do not lean on the barrier.

items.text: In front of *to* and a verb, *not* comes first and no helping verb is used.
items.example: The panel decided not to appeal.

body.heard: *Not* goes in front of the verb.
also_known_as: put not before the word you are cancelling
body.truth: It goes after the first helping verb, and the helping verb is the thing to look for. *The report not includes the site* follows the front-of-the-verb rule and is not English. *The report does not include the site* is.
body.what_to_do: Find the first helping verb and put *not* behind it. If there is no helping verb, put *do*, *does* or *did* in first.

body.mechanism: Spanish puts its negative word straight in front of the verb, and no helping verb is needed to carry it.
body.wrong: The council not approved the plan.
body.right: The council did not approve the plan.
body.fix: Put *do*, *does* or *did* in when there is no other helping verb.

body.mechanism: Chinese puts a short negative word in front of the verb, and the verb itself never changes shape.
body.wrong: She not go to the clinic last week.
body.right: She did not go to the clinic last week.
body.fix: Use *did not* for the past, and leave the verb in its plain form.
